title: A Federal Reserve Report Found That 10 Per Cent of American Households Do Not Have Enough Food. The Number Has Doubled Since 2020.
excerpt: The savings rate has dropped to 2.6 per cent. More than a third of households are dipping into savings to cover daily expenses. For immigrant families balancing costs across two countries, the squeeze is compounding.
body:
The numbers arrive quietly, buried in a Federal Reserve report that most people will never read. But the data describe something that millions of American households — including a growing number of immigrant families — are living every day.

The percentage of US households reporting that they do not have enough food to eat has doubled, from 4 per cent in June 2020 to 10 per cent in February 2026. The share of households forced to dip into personal savings to cover basic daily expenses has surged from 21.8 per cent to 36.8 per cent. Reliance on SNAP benefits has jumped from 10.6 per cent to 17.9 per cent.

And these figures were compiled before the Iran war spiked gasoline prices past $4 per gallon.

## The Savings Buffer Has Evaporated

The personal savings rate — the portion of after-tax income that Americans manage to set aside — fell to 2.6 per cent in April 2026, the lowest level since June 2022, when inflation last peaked at 9.1 per cent. A year ago, it was 5.8 per cent. Three years ago, during the stimulus era, it was above 15 per cent.

That cushion is gone.

Americans are not cutting spending. Consumer expenditure rose 0.5 per cent in April, driven by gasoline purchases and recreation. But income grew only 0.2 per cent — meaning households are spending more than they earn and covering the gap with savings, credit cards, and in some cases, retirement account withdrawals.

Credit card debt stands at $1.25 trillion, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Over half of consumers are using credit cards to cover essential spending, a May survey by debt management firm Achieve found. Nearly 5 per cent of household debt is in some stage of delinquency.

"Households do have less of a cushion now than they did two, three years ago," said Augustine Faucher, chief economist at PNC Financial. "That means this higher inflation is going to pinch more than it would have."

## The Dual-Country Squeeze for Diaspora Families

For Indian diaspora families, the financial stress carries a dimension that domestic American households do not face: obligations that span two economies.

The typical NRI family sending money home to India — whether for ageing parents, siblings' education, property maintenance, or wedding contributions — is watching the purchasing power of the dollar erode on both sides. In the United States, gasoline above $4, grocery inflation, and rising rents eat into take-home pay. In India, the rupee's volatility means the dollars they do send buy less than they expected.

The real disposable income of American households — income adjusted for inflation — fell 0.5 per cent in April alone. On a year-over-year basis, it is down 1.1 per cent, the largest annual decline since November 2022. For families maintaining financial commitments in two countries, that 1.1 per cent decline is felt twice.

Anecdotally, diaspora financial advisors report a surge in consultations from NRI families asking the same question: should they reduce remittances to protect their own emergency fund, or maintain them because the rupee is weakening?

There is no easy answer, but the data suggest that maintaining a US emergency fund is the priority. With the savings rate at 2.6 per cent and credit card balances at record highs, the margin for financial error has shrunk to nearly zero.

## Inflation Is Not Just Energy

The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index — the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge — rose 3.8 per cent year-over-year in April, the highest since May 2023. But strip away food and energy, and core inflation is still running at 3.3 per cent.

Housing and utility costs rose 0.6 per cent in a single month. Transportation services climbed 0.4 per cent. Food services and accommodations increased 0.5 per cent. This is not a gasoline-only story.

Diesel prices, which drive freight and food distribution costs, operate on a three-to-six-month lag. That means the grocery price increases from the Iran war's oil shock have not fully arrived yet.

## The Health Toll of Financial Stress

Food insecurity is not just an economic statistic. It is a health outcome. The academic literature is unambiguous: households experiencing food insecurity have higher rates of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression, and anxiety. Children in food-insecure homes show measurable deficits in cognitive development and academic performance.

For South Asian Americans, who already carry elevated cardiovascular and diabetes risk profiles compared to the general population, the combination of financial stress and poor nutrition is especially dangerous. The MASALA study — the largest longitudinal study of South Asian cardiovascular health in the United States — has documented that 30 per cent of South Asian adults have prediabetes by age 45.

A household that skips meals to make rent, or substitutes processed food for fresh produce to stretch a food budget, is not just tightening its belt. It is accumulating metabolic risk.

## What Comes Next

Markets are now pricing in a greater chance of a Federal Reserve rate hike than a rate cut in 2026, despite President Trump's repeated calls for easing. If rates rise, mortgage costs, auto loans, and credit card interest all increase — tightening the vice on households already running low on savings.

The University of Michigan consumer confidence survey hit record lows in May. Two-thirds of respondents reported cutting back on spending. When consumer sentiment falls this sharply, the effects ripple through the economy with a delay of roughly two quarters.

For immigrant families navigating the American economy, the practical steps are unglamorous but essential: build or protect a three-month emergency fund before increasing remittances, consolidate high-interest credit card debt, and defer non-essential large purchases until the inflation trajectory clarifies. The savings rate will not recover on its own. It requires deliberate action at the household level — and that starts with acknowledging that the squeeze is real.
nri_angle: NRI families face a unique dual-country financial squeeze: rising US costs (gas above $4, food inflation, rents) drain household budgets while remittance obligations to India remain fixed or growing. The savings rate collapse to 2.6% is especially dangerous for families maintaining financial commitments across two economies. Food insecurity compounds pre-existing South Asian cardiovascular and diabetes risks.
